title: Chapter 7: Fractions
summary: Equal parts, fraction names, number lines, one whole, whole numbers, fractions beyond one, and fractions of a set.

guide.title: Chapter 7 Fractions Study Guide
guide.intro: Original Study Scoop review. Define the whole first. Then count equal parts or equal number-line intervals. This guide is printable; open the self-check answers to print the answer key.

sections.title: 7-1 Equal parts
text: Partition means divide into parts. Fraction parts of one shape must have equal area. Different cuts can make valid equal shares.

examples.title: A fair share
text: A strip has four equal-area pieces. Each piece is one fourth. Four uneven pieces would not be fourths.

mistakes.mistake: Counting pieces without checking their sizes.
mistakes.fix: Check that all pieces have equal area.

checks.question: A sheet has three pieces: two small and one large. Are they thirds?
checks.answer: No. Thirds must have equal area.

sections.title: 7-2 Name the fraction
text: The denominator counts equal parts in ONE whole. The numerator counts the parts being described. A unit fraction has numerator 1.

examples.title: Selected pieces
text: This circle has six equal parts. Five are selected, so its selected fraction is 5/6.

mistakes.fix: Put the selected count on top and the number of parts in one whole below.

checks.question: Two of eight equal pieces are selected. What fraction is selected?
checks.answer: 2/8. The numerator is 2 and the denominator is 8.

sections.title: 7-3 Fractions on a number line
text: Find 0 and 1. Count the equal intervals between them, not the tick marks. Count from zero to the point to find the numerator.

examples.title: A point between zero and one
text: Four intervals fill one whole. The point is three intervals from zero, so it is 3/4.

mistakes.mistake: Using the number of tick marks as the denominator.
mistakes.fix: Count the spaces between marks from 0 to 1.

checks.question: There are seven marks including 0 and 1, evenly spaced. What denominator describes the line?
checks.answer: 6, because the seven marks enclose six equal intervals.

sections.title: 7-4 One whole
text: When every part of one whole is used, the numerator equals the denominator: b/b is one whole.

examples.title: All thirds
text: All three thirds are selected. The fraction 3/3 names one complete whole.

mistakes.fix: Six sixth-size parts together fill one whole.

checks.question: How many wholes are eight eighths?
checks.answer: One whole. All eight equal parts of the whole are present.

sections.title: 7-5 Whole numbers as fractions
text: A denominator of 1 means each part is one whole. A whole number n can be written n/1.

examples.title: Three whole units
text: Each box is one whole unit. Three whole-size parts are 3/1.

mistakes.fix: 1/3 is one small part; 3/1 is three whole-size parts.

checks.question: Write six wholes as a fraction using whole-size parts.

sections.title: 7-6 Beyond one
text: Keep the same interval size beyond 1. Count intervals from zero; the denominator stays the number of intervals in ONE whole. A numerator larger than the denominator represents more than one.

examples.title: Seven thirds
text: Each whole has three intervals. The point is seven intervals from zero, so it is 7/3. It lies between 2 and 3.

mistakes.mistake: Using every interval across the entire line as the denominator.
mistakes.fix: Only count intervals in one whole to find the denominator.

checks.question: Each whole has four intervals. A point is five intervals from zero. What fraction is it, and is it greater than one?
checks.answer: 5/4. It is greater than one because four fourths fill one whole and one fourth remains.

checks.question: Is nine fourths less than or greater than three wholes?
checks.answer: Less than three wholes. Three wholes are twelve fourths; nine fourths stop before that.

sections.title: 7-7 A fraction of a set
text: State which objects form the entire set. When each object is counted equally, the denominator is the number of objects in the whole set. A single object is a unit fraction of that set.

examples.title: A set of ten
text: All ten objects form one whole set. One selected object is 1/10 of the set. Three selected objects would be 3/10.

mistakes.mistake: Calling one object the whole when the question defines the entire set as the whole.
mistakes.fix: Read the definition of the whole before counting selected objects.

options.why: Count the sizes of the pieces, not just the number of pieces.

items.explain: Some pieces are larger than others. A fraction partition must use equal-area parts.

items.prompt: An artist cuts one square into six pieces. What must be true to call the pieces sixths?

options.text: Every piece must have a different size.
options.why: Sixths must have equal area.

options.text: Every piece must have the same area.
Every piece must be a different color.
options.why: Color does not determine equal area.

items.explain: Sixths are six equal-area pieces of one whole.

items.prompt: Two matching flags are each cut into eight equal-area pieces in different ways. What is true?

options.text: Only one arrangement can show eighths.
options.why: Different arrangements can still produce equal-area pieces.
Each flag has eight equal-area pieces.

items.explain: Eighths are eight equal-area parts; the direction of the cuts may differ.

items.prompt: The felt rectangle is one whole. Write the fraction represented by the highlighted pieces. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 8 equal parts. 7 parts are selected, so the fraction is 7/8.

items.prompt: The circular badge is one whole. Write its highlighted fraction. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 4 equal parts. 2 parts are selected, so the fraction is 2/4.

items.prompt: The banner is one whole. What is the numerator of its highlighted fraction?
items.explain: Four pieces are highlighted, so the numerator is 4.

items.prompt: A whole badge has three equal parts. One part is highlighted. Which fraction names that part?

options.why: The whole has three equal parts, not whole-size parts.
Only one part is highlighted.

items.explain: One of three equal parts is the unit fraction 1/3.

items.prompt: A robot travels from 0 to the point on this unit trail. Write its position. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 8 equal intervals. The point is 1 intervals from zero, so it represents 1/8.

items.prompt: A trail marker stands at the point. What numerator counts the equal intervals from zero to this point?
items.explain: The point is three equal intervals from zero, so the numerator is 3.

items.prompt: Count the equal spaces from 0 to 1 on this trail. What denominator do they give?
items.explain: Six intervals fill the whole from 0 to 1, so the denominator is 6.

items.prompt: A robot trail has nine equally spaced marks including 0 and 1. How many equal intervals lie between 0 and 1?

options.why: Count spaces between neighboring marks.
Nine marks enclose eight spaces.

items.explain: There are eight intervals between nine boundary marks.

items.prompt: Every piece of this round lantern panel is highlighted. Write the fraction using its partition. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 6 equal parts. 6 parts are selected, so the fraction is 6/6.

items.prompt: Every piece of this circular collage is highlighted. Write the fraction shown. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 8 equal parts. 8 parts are selected, so the fraction is 8/8.

items.prompt: Which fraction can name one complete lantern panel?

options.why: Only one sixth is named.
One sixth is missing.

items.explain: All six sixths make exactly one whole.

items.prompt: All three equal pieces of a collage are used. How many complete collages do those three thirds make?
items.explain: All 3 of the 3 equal pieces fill the original one collage.

items.prompt: Each stage block is one whole. Write the selected whole blocks as a fraction with denominator 1. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 1 equal parts. 5 parts are selected, so the fraction is 5/1.

items.prompt: Each interval is one whole platform-length. Write the marked position as a fraction with denominator 1. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 1 equal intervals. The point is 2 intervals from zero, so it represents 2/1.

items.prompt: Which fraction writes seven whole platforms using whole-size parts?

options.why: One seventh is part of one platform.
Seven sevenths fill only one whole.

items.explain: Seven whole-size parts are written 7/1.

items.prompt: A stage builder writes 8/1 for a count of whole blocks. How many whole blocks is that?
items.explain: Eight parts of size one whole make 8 whole blocks.

items.prompt: A hiking marker lies at this point. Write its fraction using the equal intervals shown. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 4 equal intervals. The point is 9 intervals from zero, so it represents 9/4.

items.prompt: A hiker reaches the marked point. Write its fraction. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 6 equal intervals. The point is 11 intervals from zero, so it represents 11/6.

items.prompt: Write the marked distance on this hiking line as a fraction. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: Each whole has 8 equal intervals. The point is 11 intervals from zero, so it represents 11/8.

items.prompt: The marked hiking distance is compared with 4 wholes. Which statement is true?

options.why: The point lies before 4.
Four wholes would take twelve thirds.

items.explain: The point is 11/3. Four wholes take 12 thirds, so 11 thirds is less than 4.

items.prompt: These twelve seeds form one whole set. Write the fraction selected. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: The whole set has 12 objects. 1 objects are selected, so the selected fraction is 1/12.

items.prompt: All ten buttons are one whole set. Write the selected fraction. Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: The whole set has 10 objects. 3 objects are selected, so the selected fraction is 3/10.

items.prompt: The five seeds are the entire set. The selected seeds have not sprouted. What fraction of the set has not sprouted? Use the number of parts in one whole shown by the model as your denominator.
items.explain: The whole set has 5 objects. 2 objects are selected, so the selected fraction is 2/5.

items.prompt: A whole set has four buttons. What fraction of the entire set is one button?

options.why: The whole is all four buttons, not a single button.
Only one button is being described.

items.explain: One of four equally counted objects is 1/4 of the whole set.

performance.title: Plan a fraction art display
performance.note: Optional, ungraded original task. Explain your reasoning aloud or on paper. Compare your work with the examples; this is not a teacher-assigned test.

tasks.prompt: The entire strip is one whole display panel. Name the highlighted fraction and explain what each number means.
tasks.example: 3/8: the whole panel has eight equal parts, and three are highlighted.

tasks.prompt: A second panel uses all six of its sixth-size pieces. Write the fraction and explain how much of one whole panel it covers.
tasks.example: 6/6 covers exactly one whole panel because every one of its six parts is used.

tasks.prompt: A decoration reaches the marked point on the display rail. Write its fraction and explain why it is beyond one.
tasks.example: 7/4. Four fourth-size intervals make one whole. Seven such intervals go past one whole.

tasks.prompt: All five clips make one whole set. Write the fraction of clips selected for the display.
tasks.example: 2/5 of the set is selected: two selected clips out of five clips in the whole set.
